title: Science experiment for Year 12 students
subject: listening

paragraphs.text: Jake Hi Jake. How are you getting on with the practical teaching?
Jake: It’s harder than I expected, but I’ve got some great classes. How about you?
Clare: Not brilliant. I’m really struggling with my Year 12 science class.
Jake: Are they hard to control?
Clare: Well, I don’t have discipline problems as such. It’s just that they don’t seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives. It’s depressing.
Clare: They listen to what I say, and I gave them a test last week and the results weren’t too bad, but there’s no real engagement.
Jake: Right.
Clare: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do.
Clare: I was wondering about something on the children’s diets . . . you know, asking them to record what they eat and maybe linking it to their state of health.
Jake: Mmm. Let’s think. So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat.
Jake: OK, but you’d also need to have access to the children’s medical records and I don’t think people would be happy about that; confidentiality would be an issue.
Jake: If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it’s not going to be easy.
Clare: Right.
Jake: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?
Clare: Wouldn’t that be upsetting for the children?
Jake: Well, the animals don’t have to be harmed in any way. It could just be an experiment where they’re given a certain diet and the effects are observed.
Clare: Would I have to get permission to use animals?
Jake: Yes, you’d have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form, but it’s quite straightforward.
Clare: But if we found out that, say, a particular diet affects the health of animals,
the same thing wouldn’t necessarily be true for people, would it?
Jake: No that’s true, but the findings for any experiment are going to be limited. It’s inevitable.
Clare: I suppose so. So what animals could I use to investigate the effects of diet? Mice?
Jake: Yes. You’d need experimental mice – ones that have been specially bred for experiments.
Jake: OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?
Clare: Well, something to do with nutrition. So maybe we could look at food supplements . . . things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.
Jake: Mmm. That might be rather broad. Maybe just look at the effects of one supplement, like sugar, on the health of the mice?
Clare: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet. . . .
Jake: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar, that they don’t really need?
Clare: Exactly. Do they eat it or do they decide to leave it?
Jake: Great. Then later on, you could do a follow-up experiment adding another variable.
Jake: Like, you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active, running on a wheel or something, and the others just sit around and don’t do much.
Clare: Or I could repeat the experiment but change the type of food I provided . . . or use mice with a different genetic structure.
Clare: But I think your idea would be more interesting, I might think about that some more.
Clare: So can I talk through a possible procedure for the experiment where mice are given a sugar supplement?
Jake: Sure. I did a similar experiment in college actually.
Clare: Great. So how many mice would I need?
Jake: I’d say about 12. And all young ones, not a mixture of old and young.
Clare: OK. And I’d need two groups of equal sizes, so six in each group. And how would I tell them apart?
Clare: I suppose I could put some sort of tag on one group . . . or just mark them in some way?
Jake: You could use food colouring, that wouldn’t hurt them.
Clare: Perfect. Then each group would go into a separate cage, and one group, let’s call them group A, would be the control group.
Clare: So they’d just have ordinary mouse food. I suppose you can buy that?
Jake: Yes, it comes in dry pellets.
Clare: And the other group would have the same as the first group, but they’d also have the extra sugar.
Jake: Would you just give them straight sugar?
Clare: It might be better to give them something like cereal with it.
Jake: Mmm. Then you’d need to weigh the mice, I should think once a week. And you’d need an electronic balance.
Clare: But we can’t hold them on the balance, or it’d affect the reading.
Jake: Exactly. So you need something called a weighing chamber to stop the mice from running away.
Jake: It sounds complicated, but actually you can just use a plastic box with holes in the top.
Clare: OK. So once we’ve measured the weight gain of each mouse we can work out the average for each group, as well as the standard deviation.
Clare: And then see where we go from there. That sounds cool, I think the students will enjoy it.
Jake: Yes. One thing . . .

groups.instruction:
Questions 21–25

Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

Science experiment for Year 12 students

questions.prompt: How does Clare feel about the students in her Year 12 science class?

options.text: worried that they are not making progress
challenged by their poor behaviour in class
frustrated at their lack of interest in the subject

questions.explanation: 本题题干问题中的Year 12 science class在原文中原词重现，大致定位。接下来Jake的问题中提及是否hard to control，对应B选项，但Clare给出了否定回复don’t have discipline problems as such，discipline意为“纪律”，discipline problems对应B选项中的poor behaviour，as such指“从字面意义看，严格来说”，否定回复排除B。接下来Clare说don’t seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives，这里的science对应C选项中的subject，其他信息对应lack of interest。下一句中depressing意为“令人沮丧的”，对应C选项中的frustrated。因此本题答案为C。

questions.prompt: How does Jake react to Clare’s suggestion about an experiment based on children’s diet?

options.text: He is concerned that the results might not be meaningful.
He feels some of the data might be difficult to obtain.
He suspects that the conclusions might be upsetting.

questions.explanation: 本题题干问题中的experiment和children’s diet在原文中原词重现，大致定位。需要注意本题问的是Jake对于Clare的建议做出的回应，react意为“回应，作出反应”。原文中Clare说到的record以及Jake说到的recording和records，可以对应B选项中的data。Jake的回应中，在but之后说到need to have access…以及don’t think…happy about that，以及confidentiality，意为“保密性，机密性”，这些都是B选项中difficult to obtain的具体表现，即数据难以获得。在之后的内容中，虽然conclusions原词重现，且出现了suspect对应C选项中的suspect，但相关表述为significant和not going to be easy，与C中的upsetting不符合，upsetting意为“令人不快（或忧虑、苦恼）的”。同时，原文中的significant与A选项中的not…meaningful相互矛盾，meaningful意为“重要的，意义明显的”。因此排除C和A，本题答案为B。

questions.prompt: What problem do they agree may be involved in an experiment involving animals?

options.text: Any results may not apply to humans.
It may be complicated to get permission.
Students may not be happy about animal experiments.

questions.explanation: 本题题干问题中的experiment和animals在原文中原词重现，大致定位。需要注意原文中提及与选项的相关内容，是否符合题干中的agree。原文中Clare先问到upsetting，对应C选项中的not…happy，但Jake的回应是the animals don’t have to be harmed，此处内容不符合agree，排除C。接下来Clare问到get permission的相关问题，B选项部分关键词原词重现，但Jake回答说该操作十分straightforward，意为“简单的，不复杂的”，与B选项中的complicated不符，故排除B。之后Clare的表述found out对应A选项中的results，wouldn’t necessarily be true for people对应A选项中的may not apply to humans。结合Jake回应中but之后的the findings…limited，以及Clare进一步的回应“I suppose so.”表现出两人关于这一问题意见达成一致。因此本题答案为A。

questions.prompt: What question do they decide the experiment should address?

options.text: Are mice capable of controlling their food intake?
Does an increase in sugar lead to health problems?
How much do supplements of different kinds affect health?

questions.explanation: 本题需要注意题干问题中的address用作动词，表示“设法解决，处理”，而非名词的“地址”。原文中Jake提出的问题…what will your experiment be investigating exactly对应本题题干。Clare在回复中首先提及nutrition，意为“营养”，之后supplements原词重现，对应C选项，意为“添加物，补充（物）”，原文中的例子extra iron和extra protein代表C选项中的different kinds，原文中的impact on health对应C选项中的affect health。但从Jake的回应Mmm以及rather broad可以看出，这并不是两人达成一致的决定，故排除C。紧跟着Jake问到sugar对于老鼠健康的影响，对应B选项，但Clare对此没有给出肯定回复，而是转而谈论其他方面的内容，故排除B。Clare讲到的是…whether mice can control their own diet，原文中的whether对应A选项中Are…capable of…，control对应A选项中的controlling，diet对应food intake。接下来的原文中，两人对话中的what happens…以及eat it or…leave it，进一步体现出了A选项的内容，两人的回应Exactly和Great表现出对这一问题达成了一致意见。因此本题答案为A。

questions.prompt: Clare might also consider doing another experiment involving

options.text: other types of food supplement.
different geneticstrains of mice.
varying amounts of exercise.

questions.explanation: 本题题干中的experiment和another在原文中原词重现，原文中的follow-up在这里可以理解为“进一步的”，这一表述还有“后续行动，后续事物”的意思。原文中Jake讲到的variable意为“变量，可变因素”，加上之后讲到的具体内容，一些老鼠more active, running on a wheel or something，另一些老鼠sit around and don’t do much，对应C选项中的varying amounts of exercise。接下来Clare虽然提到change the type of food I provided，对应A选项；还提到different genetic structure，对应B选项，但之后出现了转折But，表示Jake的想法更有意思，也就是肯定了前面Jake讲到的C选项。因此本题答案为C。

Questions 26–30

Complete the flowchart below.

Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–H, next to Questions 26–30.

questions.prompt: Choose mice which are all the same [26] ______.
questions.explanation:
26. 题干中的all在原文中原词重现，原文为all young ones，ones指代前面讲到的mice，紧接着出现否定相关信息not a mixture of old and young。young和old对应C选项age，all young ones以及对于实验中老鼠老幼混合的否定，对应题干中空前的same。因此本题答案为C。

27. 题干中的two groups在原文中原词重现，之后提及equal sizes。equal与题干中空前的different不符，故排除A选项size。在问到如何区分数量同为6只的两组老鼠时，Clare先讲到put some sort of tag或mark them in some way，Jake在回应中讲到使用不会伤害到老鼠的food colouring，意思是“食物着色剂”，Clare对此给出肯定的回应。colouring对应H选项的colour，因此本题答案为H。

28. 本题先结合原文中的Then定位到流程图中的下一步。在空格之前的两行题干中，each group，separate cage，group A以及mouse food在原文中都原词重现，原文中ordinary mouse food对应题干中的commercial mouse food。接下来原文中the other group对应题干中的group B，sugar原词重现，定位在空格所在行。之后Clare讲到give them something like cereal with it这样更好，cereal即本题答案，意为“谷物，谷类食物”。因此本题答案为E。

29. 本题空格上一行中的measurement意为“（某物的）尺寸，长度，数量”，scale意为“秤”。原文中weigh对应题干中的Take measurements，原文中electronic balance对应题干中的electronic scale。weighing chamber原词重现，原文中的stop…from对应空前的prevent，接下来的running away对应B选项的escape。因此本题答案为B。

30. 原文中先提及与29题相关的测量内容，之后说到work out the average以及standard deviation。work out sth.或work sth. out意为“计算，算出”，average表示“平均数”，standard deviation指“标准差，标准偏差”，都对应F选项中的calculations，意为“计算”。因此本题答案为F。

groups.contextHtml:
Choose mice which are all the same [26] ______.

 Divide the mice into two groups, each with a different [27] ______.

 Put each group in a separate cage. 

 Feed group A commercial mouse food.

 Feed group B the same, but also sugar contained in [28] ______. 

 Take measurements using an electronic scale.

 Place them in a weighing chamber to prevent [29] ______.

 Do all necessary [30] ______.

transcriptHtml:
Jake Hi Jake. How are you getting on with the practical teaching?

Jake: It’s harder than I expected, but I’ve got some great classes. How about you?

Clare: Not brilliant. I’m really struggling with my Year 12 science class.

Jake: Are they hard to control?

Clare: Well, I don’t have discipline problems as such. It’s just that they don’t seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives. It’s depressing. 

Clare: They listen to what I say, and I gave them a test last week and the results weren’t too bad, but there’s no real engagement.

Jake: Right.

Clare: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do. 

Clare: I was wondering about something on the children’s diets . . . you know, asking them to record what they eat and maybe linking it to their state of health.

Jake: Mmm. Let’s think. So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat. 

Jake: OK, but you’d also need to have access to the children’s medical records and I don’t think people would be happy about that; confidentiality would be an issue.

Jake:  If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it’s not going to be easy.

Clare: Right.

Jake: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?

Clare: Wouldn’t that be upsetting for the children?

Jake: Well, the animals don’t have to be harmed in any way. It could just be an experiment where they’re given a certain diet and the effects are observed.

Clare: Would I have to get permission to use animals?

Jake: Yes, you’d have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form, but it’s quite straightforward.

Clare: But if we found out that, say, a particular diet affects the health of animals,

the same thing wouldn’t necessarily be true for people, would it?

Jake: No that’s true, but the findings for any experiment are going to be limited. It’s inevitable.

Clare: I suppose so. So what animals could I use to investigate the effects of diet? Mice?

Jake: Yes. You’d need experimental mice – ones that have been specially bred for experiments.

Jake: OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?

Clare: Well, something to do with nutrition. So maybe we could look at food supplements . . . things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.

Jake: Mmm. That might be rather broad. Maybe just look at the effects of one supplement, like sugar, on the health of the mice?

Clare: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet. . . .

Jake: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar, that they don’t really need?

Clare: Exactly. Do they eat it or do they decide to leave it?

Jake: Great. Then later on, you could do a follow-up experiment adding another variable. 

Jake: Like, you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active, running on a wheel or something, and the others just sit around and don’t do much.

Clare: Or I could repeat the experiment but change the type of food I provided . . . or use mice with a different genetic structure.
